questions.prompt: Which function reads the property `env` with a default of `qa`?
options: ${__P(env,qa)}
${env}
${__V(env,qa)}
%env%
questions.explanation: __P reads a property with an optional default. ${env} reads a variable, __V evaluates a variable name expression, and %env% is Windows shell syntax.

questions.prompt: Which command-line option sets a JMeter property for a local run?
options: -Jname=value
-Dname=value only
-Vname=value
-Pname=value
questions.explanation: -J sets a JMeter property. -D sets a Java system property, -p (lowercase) names a properties file, and -V does not exist.

questions.prompt: JMeter variables are local to each thread.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own copy of variables. Properties are global to the JMeter instance.

questions.prompt: The test is started with `jmeter -n -t plan.jmx -Jhost=staging.local`. What host is used?
options: staging.local
localhost
${__P(host,localhost)} literally
An error, because the property is undefined
questions.explanation: The property is defined on the command line, so __P returns it instead of the default.

questions.prompt: A setUp Thread Group fetches an admin token that every user thread needs. How should it be shared?
options: Save it as a property, e.g. props.put('adminToken', token), and read it with ${__P(adminToken)} in the main groups
Save it as a variable; variables are shared between Thread Groups
Put it in User Defined Variables at run time
Write it to jmeter.log and read it back
questions.explanation: Properties cross threads and groups; variables do not. User Defined Variables are evaluated at start-up, so cannot capture a later value, and reading logs is fragile.

questions.prompt: Which statements about User Defined Variables are correct? Select all that apply.
options: They are processed at the start of the test regardless of where they are placed
They are suited to static configuration values
They should not contain functions that must produce a new value per request
They can only be placed under a sampler
questions.explanation: The manual notes UDVs are processed once at start-up, so use them for configuration; per-request functions belong in sampler fields or pre-processors. They can be placed in many locations, typically the Test Plan.

questions.prompt: A request goes to `/users/${userId}` literally. A JSON Extractor names the variable `userID` and has no default value. What happened?
options: The variable names differ in case (userId vs userID); JMeter names are case-sensitive and an undefined variable is left as the literal text
JMeter only substitutes variables in the Server Name
The extractor needs a Constant Timer
The path must be URL-encoded first
questions.explanation: Undefined variable references are left as-is, and names are case-sensitive. Variables work in any field, timers are unrelated, and encoding does not define the variable.

questions.prompt: You must run the same plan against dev (50 users) and staging (500 users) in CI without editing the .jmx. Which design works best?
options: Use ${__P(threads,5)} and ${__P(host,localhost)} in the plan, and pass -Jthreads/-Jhost (or a -q env properties file) per environment
Keep two copies of the .jmx
Use a CSV file with one row per environment
Edit jmeter.properties on each agent
questions.explanation: Properties with defaults keep one plan and let the pipeline choose values; a small default keeps local runs safe. Copies drift, CSV rows are per-thread data, and editing jmeter.properties is fragile and global.

coding.title: Resolve ${var} and ${__P()} references
coding.prompt:
Write `resolve(text, variables, properties)` that replaces:

- `${name}` with `variables[name]` if defined, otherwise leaves the reference unchanged (as JMeter does).
- `${__P(name)}` or `${__P(name,default)}` with `properties[name]` if defined, else the default, else `'1'` (JMeter's __P default when none is given).

Names are case-sensitive. Example: `resolve('http://${__P(host,localhost)}/u/${id}', {'id': '7'}, {})` returns `'http://localhost/u/7'`.
coding.explanation: Two regex passes mirror JMeter's behaviour: property functions fall back to their default, and unknown variables stay literal, which is exactly the clue you look for when a request URL contains `${...}`.
hints: Handle `__P` first with one regex, then plain variables with another.
`re.sub` accepts a function, so you can decide the replacement per match.
For unknown variables return `m.group(0)` to keep the original text.

coding.title: Thread-local variables versus global properties
coding.prompt:
Simulate JMeter's storage. Write a class `Jmeter` with:

- `props`: one dict shared by all threads.
- `vars_for(thread_id)`: returns that thread's own dict (created on first use, then the same dict every time).

Example: setting `vars_for(1)['token'] = 'a'` must not make `'token'` appear in `vars_for(2)`, but `props['token'] = 'a'` is seen by everyone.
coding.explanation: Keeping one dict per thread id models JMeterVariables (thread-local), while a single shared dict models JMeter properties. It explains why an extracted token cannot be read by another thread through a variable.
hints: Create `props` and a dict of per-thread dicts in `__init__`.
`dict.setdefault(key, {})` returns the existing dict or creates one.
Return the same dict object each time so changes persist.

tests.name: Variables are per thread
tests.code:
j = Jmeter()
j.vars_for(1)['token'] = 'a'
assert 'token' not in j.vars_for(2) and j.vars_for(1)['token'] == 'a'

tests.name: Properties are shared
tests.code:
j = Jmeter()
j.props['env'] = 'qa'
assert j.props == {'env': 'qa'}
assert j.vars_for(1) is j.vars_for(1)
